source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: The Importance of the Close of the Bar

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant).

candidates.name: WeakFollowThroughScalpExit
candidates.quote: If the entry bar is six ticks tall, you would much prefer seeing the body suddenly increase from a body that was two ticks to one that was four ticks in the final seconds of the bar... This is true for the next couple of bars as well. If there are strong closes, you should be more willing to swing more contracts and hold them for more points than if these bars had weak closes.
candidates.description: The chapter's one genuinely bar-level, position-management idea: how strongly the entry bar and the bar right after it close (in the trade's direction) should govern whether to take a quick scalp or hold for a larger target. Since this engine has no position-sizing primitive, the sizing decision is mechanized as a binary exit: take the available profit now (a quick scalp) when the entry bar or the very next bar did NOT close as a strong trend bar in the trade's direction; otherwise let it run toward a larger target.
candidates.pseudocode: n = ctx.BarsSinceEntry(); entryBarWeak = (close[n] - open[n]) < strongBodyFraction * (high[n] - low[n]) || close[n] <= open[n]; nextBarWeak = (n >= 1) && ((close[n-1] - open[n-1]) < strongBodyFraction * (high[n-1] - low[n-1]) || close[n-1] <= open[n-1]); (n == 0 && entryBarWeak) || (n == 1 && nextBarWeak) && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() > 0
candidates.book_order_type: exit at the market (or scale out) as soon as the weak close is confirmed, rather than holding for a larger swing target

complexity.reason: needs to index back to the entry bar and the bar right after it using BarsSinceEntry, and reuses the corpus's trend-bar body-fraction test

notes: This is an approximation: Brooks's actual point is about position SIZE (how many contracts to hold/scale out), which the engine's Entry/Exit boolean framework cannot express directly; it is recast here as a binary quick-scalp-vs-hold exit decision.
The rest of this short chapter is almost entirely about intrabar (sub-bar) price behavior in the final seconds before a bar closes, which is data below the bar and is rejected below.

chapter_summary: A short, mostly cautionary chapter: don't act on a bar's apparent shape before it closes, and don't move stops or bail out based on intrabar price wiggling in the final seconds -- both the early-entry temptation and the getting-stopped-out-then-missing-the-move examples are fundamentally about sub-bar (tick-level) price action that this bar-close-only engine cannot see, so nearly the whole chapter is rejected on that basis. The one bar-level idea worth keeping is that the strength of the entry bar's close and the bar right after it should govern whether to scalp out quickly or hold for a bigger target (T08-01), recast here as a binary exit since the engine has no position-sizing concept. The chapter also argues, via a 3-minute-vs-5-minute chart comparison, that trading a smaller bar interval increases stop-run risk relative to a larger one -- a timeframe-choice heuristic rather than a per-bar rule, so it is rejected too rather than forced into a spurious condition.
